structure.title: Part I, chapters 1–16 · Assemble the parts of a political person
structure.text: Hobbes begins with sense, imagination, words and appetite. By the time two people want the same scarce thing, he has equipped them with memory, expectations and reasons to fear each other's preparations long before either has struck.

structure.title: Part II, chapters 17–31 · How can a multitude act as one?
structure.text: Covenants and representation make a commonwealth possible. Its sovereign must be able to decide disputes whose settlement would otherwise depend on whichever party could enforce its own interpretation. Tax, counsel and punishment give this abstract requirement practical consequences.

structure.title: Part III, chapters 32–43 · Who may speak for God in public?
structure.text: Hobbes reads Scripture at length to determine what authority a Christian subject may recognise alongside the civil sovereign. A claim to interpret divine commands can reopen, inside a commonwealth, the very struggle over final judgment that sovereignty was supposed to settle.

structure.title: Part IV, chapter 44 – A Review and Conclusion · Trace the interests behind darkness
structure.text: Misreading Scripture, inherited philosophical vocabulary and clerical claims come under sustained attack. A book that began with how words acquire meaning ends up asking who benefits when people use words they cannot explain.

people.name: The sovereign
people.role: A person or assembly authorised to represent many
people.text: Hobbes wants a decision that subjects can recognise as their own authorised act even when they oppose it. Representation gives his commonwealth a single voice and raises a difficult question about the limits of what a person can authorise.

people.name: The covenant
people.role: A promise whose performance may come later
people.text: Going first can leave someone defenceless if the other party never performs. Hobbes's concern with enforcement grows from this interval between two performances and the reasonable suspicions that fit inside it.

people.name: Natural liberty
people.role: A person's use of power for self-preservation
people.text: A subject can surrender many freedoms for the sake of peace. Hobbes pays special attention to cases, such as an immediate threat to life, where the rationale for submission strains against the demand to obey.

context.title: England's wars and divided loyalties
context.text: Civil and religious claims to obedience could direct the same person toward incompatible actions. This gives urgency to Hobbes's apparently dry question of who may settle the meaning of a written command.

context.title: The state of nature is a test
context.text: Hobbes asks what security people could achieve without a common power. His argument can be examined by considering whether fear and mutual vulnerability would persist even among people who generally preferred peaceful lives.

notice.text: Watch the peaceful neighbour lock the door.
notice.why: Hobbes appeals to ordinary precautions as evidence about expectations. The lock says something about what someone dares trust, even if the owner would describe most neighbours as decent.

On a stage one person speaks in another's name. Hobbes turns that distinction into an account of responsibility for political acts, where the words of a representative can count as the act of thousands.

opening: Two people can both want peace and still have reasons to attack first. Neither can be certain the other will keep a promise, and waiting may leave them defenceless. Hobbes builds his account of government from that predicament, amid the experience of civil war. The authority capable of ending fear must be powerful enough to make obedience safer than resistance. Following the argument means confronting how much power people might surrender for protection, and what remains of the bargain when protection fails.
